Le mur Facebook de Carlos Rojas est un f: Carlos Rojas's Facebook wall is a constant stream of information for the community that follows him, interspersed with messages of kindness and calls to action on climate change. His social media reflects the way of life of this Mexican-Quebecer, who splits his days between a 9-to-5 job and volunteering on behalf of migrants with precarious status.
Carlos est cofondateur et directeur de C: Carlos is co-founder and director of Conseil migrant, a Montréal-based non-profit that helps people with precarious status, asylum seekers and temporary workers.
Mais le travail de cet administrateur d': But the work of this business administrator, trained at the Tecnológico de Monterrey (the Mexican Harvard), goes well beyond that. It is common to see him on his social media asking for help getting a medical appointment for someone without status, or taking part in demonstrations calling for the regularization of undocumented people.
Ce grand gaillard à la voix chaleureuse: This tall man with a warm voice and gentle gestures doesn't define himself as an activist or a militant, but he passionately supports the organizations that take on that role on behalf of migrants, especially now that the Canadian government has <l1>announced a plan to regularize undocumented people</l1>.
« Il y a des centaines d'organisations à: “There are hundreds of organizations across Canada that have synchronized with a positive energy to take part,” he says, referring to the recent petitions the organizations have published, demanding details from Marc Miller, Canada's Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, about the regularization plan announced in November and promised for this spring. <l1>A program that would nonetheless be called into question, we learned on March 25</l1>. In this regard, Carlos Rojas warned that “it was a missed opportunity, because [without the regularization of undocumented people] society will continue to have a fictitious economy and undocumented people will continue to be victims of abuse.”
Ces organisations font entendre leur voi: These organizations are making their voices heard in a pre-election context in Canada, where political discourse has permeated public opinion to the point that, according to polls, 50% of the Canadian population believes there are too many immigrants.
« La vérité c’est que l'immigration est: “The truth is that immigration has become a hostage to political causes, and the big problem is that Canada is buying into a discourse that doesn't fit it.”
Pour ce spécialiste du commerce internat: For this specialist in international trade and climate change, the connection with migrants began in the United States, where he studied for several years at Columbia University before working at the Mexican consulate. Looking back, Carlos acknowledges that he was headed for a different professional career.
« Je suis le premier de ma famille à all: “I'm the first in my family to go to university, thanks to my parents' work and a scholarship (...). I was heading into a completely different environment, in business. When I left to study climate change in the United States, I saw another way of life. That's where I discovered my country, curiously, outside of Mexico, through the voices of migrants. That's also where I got to know many countries of the Americas, because I was face to face with migrants from everywhere, who had crossed the desert,” he recalls with a certain nostalgia.
Lorsqu'on lui demande pourquoi il consac: When asked why he devotes part of his life to defending migrants with precarious status, Carlos mentions one story, one of the thousands he has collected over more than 20 years.
« Lorsque j'étais aux États-Unis, j'ai e: “When I was in the United States, I moved into an apartment with a roommate. One day, he suggested we go to McDonald's (...). At the end of the meal, he ordered two more meals for the next day. On the way home, we were in the car and he saw a man on the road. He asked him how he was doing, and whether he had just arrived (as an immigrant), and the man said yes. He asked him if he had a place to sleep and if he had eaten. Since he hadn't, my friend offered him a ride. He showed him where to find help, where to sleep, and gave him the extra food he had bought. That was the end of the exchange. When I asked him why he was doing all this for someone else, he answered: because someone did it for me when I arrived .”
Carlos a autant d'histoires que les migr: Carlos has as many stories as the migrants he has met along the way. Although some of them are public, since he has shared them on his social media, he prefers not to give names or anecdotes “because I don't have permission.” When he talks about the people without status he has dealt with in emergency situations, the circumstances are such that simply recounting the events brings tears to his eyes.
Les situations d'urgence vécues par les: The emergencies faced by migrants with precarious status, including the temporary workers Carlos Rojas and his team mobilize for, are generally related to health services and legal services.
Montréal a été déclarée ville sanctuaire: Montréal was declared a sanctuary city in February 2017, which means that all members of a community can access city services without being questioned about their immigration status. In practice, however, it is very difficult for undocumented people to access these services.
Selon les données de 2017, Montréal abri: According to 2017 data, Montréal was home that year to some 50,000 undocumented people, or 10% of the total number of undocumented people in Canada.
« Le fait même que nous ne disposions pa: “The very fact that we don't have recent studies shows a lack of interest and an absence of strategic thinking. The only study that was done, and that the government still cites nearly ten years later, indicates that there were about 500,000 undocumented immigrants in Canada. That figure could be one million today.” “You have to be careful with that number, because the idea is not to scare people,” he says, but rather to show how necessary immigrants are, because they are the ones who make the engine of the Canadian economy run, in part. For Carlos, “undocumented migrants are de facto slaves.”
Qu’entend-il par « esclaves » ? « Ce son: What does he mean by “slaves”? “These are people who have no rights,” he warns. “People and Quebecers don't understand and don't know what these people do for them. The tomatoes you eat are bloodstained. Every year, every harvest season, three or four migrant workers die, and these are preventable deaths. Farm workers are three, four, five times more likely to die. Behind your clean desk is the story of someone who worked all night, a person who maybe had dreams, ideas, desires, and so on, and who comes and is limited to this. When you call your bank and someone answers, it's probably a professional who couldn't find another job,” he explains. His irritation as he talks about these circumstances shows on his face.
« Nous avons une vie qui est très agréab: “We have a very pleasant life, but it's built on the suffering of many people,” he adds.
Le profil de ces personnes n'est pas hom: The profile of these people is not uniform, something Carlos is keen to stress. “When we talk about people without status, or with precarious status, we immediately imagine a very particular type of person. In reality, it's a true rainbow of people. We've met all kinds: the partner of a doctoral student in a field of strategic interest to Canada, whose insurance covered only him and not her, people who ended up without status because of bureaucratic errors. Things aren't as black and white as many would like us to believe.”
<strong>« La plus grande force du Canada: “Canada's greatest strength right now is immigration”
Malgré les conditions dans lesquelles vi: Despite the conditions in which thousands of people with precarious status live, for Carlos Rojas, the Canadian immigration system works. It isn't that it's optimal, but he considers that, compared with other countries, it is a system that works, at least in welcoming migrants. “And we saw it in 2017, with the 50,000 people who came from the United States. We didn't see people on the streets. Canada has a good system compared with other countries,” he repeats.
Mais le directeur du Conseil Migrant ass: But the director of Conseil Migrant insists that work is urgently needed to regularize migrants without status, and to improve the living conditions of temporary workers and of everyone with precarious status in Canada.
« Les conflits internationaux obligent l: “International conflicts are forcing countries to reorient their economies. The United States seems to be in a war economy: they're bringing industries back home, lowering requirements to recruit for the military. Conflicts are on the agenda everywhere. Right now, Canada's greatest strength is immigration,” he stresses.
Afin de réformer le système d'immigratio: To reform the Canadian immigration system, more research in this area is needed. “Migration is one of the oldest phenomena, but also one of the least studied. It's a field that deserves its own area of study, degrees in migrant integration or even migration engineering,” he explains.
Outre les experts, il est nécessaire que: Beyond experts, society needs to finally recognize undocumented or precarious immigration, which is also what Conseil migrant is working toward.
« Il faut que le public comprenne que l': “The public needs to understand that immigration is not a problem, as some claim. Canada is a country of migrants. And the truth is that the country's future will continue to grow thanks to migrants. Even if new Canadians have a lot of children, we need other people to come and settle in Canada. But we also need to improve the system with a humanitarian vision.”
Sans avoir de boule de cristal, Carlos R: Without a crystal ball, Carlos Rojas believes people will keep coming. And that's despite deportations and the <l1>dangerous journeys exiles expose themselves to, such as the Darien</l1>, the crossing of the Rio Grande or the extreme temperatures of North America. Hence the importance of acting now, he believes.
« Nous devons élargir les possibilités a: “We have to widen the possibilities so that the people who will come anyway aren't left behind, so we don't make them invisible. We must not force them to live on the margins of the law. That amounts to giving more power to criminal groups. When Roxham Road was closed, the only thing we did was increase the fees in Tijuana for the people who bring French-speaking immigrants to Quebec. That's what's going to happen, for example, with the new visa requirement for Mexicans. We can't repeat the failed policies of the United States,” he says.
Carlos Rojas est convaincu qu'il vit dan: Carlos Rojas is convinced that he lives in a country of opportunities. He himself came to Canada as an immigrant under the skilled workers program. When people tell him he doesn't like Quebec because he is critical of the system, he replies that it's because he loves this province and this country; he wants it to keep getting better and better.
